study_identification_part.si4_title: A 10-Year Longitudinal Study of Brain Cortical Thickness in People with FirstEpisode Psychosis Using Normative Models

cm1_research_objectives.reason: The abstract and introduction explicitly state the aim to characterize longitudinal cortical changes in first-episode psychosis and relate normative-model deviations to symptoms over 10 years, describing why normative modeling is applied to track clinical trajectories.
cm1_research_objectives.supporting_text: “we aimed to characterize the temporal evolution of cortical correlates of psychosis and their associations with symptoms… Normative models… were applied… Then, we assessed the association between CT deviations and symptom scales”

nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.reason: Eligibility for healthy controls (language, IQ>70, no severe head trauma or major psychiatric/substance history) and patient diagnoses are described, and MRI quality control excluded Euler >5. Final sample sizes for controls at each wave are reported. However, detailed exclusion counts and criteria for the large public reference datasets used to train the normative model are not provided.
nm1_selection_criteria_reference_cohort.supporting_text: “Healthy CTRL from the same geographic catchment area were invited… Exclusion criteria for healthy CTRL included a history of drug or alcohol abuse or dependency, psychosis, bipolar disorder, or major depressive disorder, or having a first-degree relative diagnosed with a psychotic or bipolar disorder.” / “Patients… had no history of severe head trauma, and had an IQ above 70.” / “samples with a value higher than 5 were removed.” / “N 218…197…77”

nm2_handling_of_covariates_reference_coh.reason: Normative models included age as a covariate and modeled sex and scanner ID as batch effects within hierarchical Bayesian regression to address site/scanner variation.
nm2_handling_of_covariates_reference_coh.supporting_text: “using HBR with age as a covariate, and sex and scanner id as batch effects, to predict CT… This accommodated multisite pooling using transfer learning and comparisons across scanners.”

nm3_data_sources_reference_cohort.reason: The reference normative models were trained on pooled data from mostly publicly available datasets spanning 77 sites with 40,435 participants, and then adapted to three Oslo scanners using held-out local controls.
nm3_data_sources_reference_cohort.supporting_text: “Using pooled data from a collection of mostly publicly available datasets from 77 sites, and 40 435 participants… We then adapted the model to the 3 unseen Oslo scanners… using held-out cross-sectional data from CTRL from these 3 scanners.”

nm4_image_acquisition_protocol.reason: Three MRI scanners (1.5T Siemens Sonata, 3T GE Signa HDxT, 3T GE 750 Discovery) are described with coil types and key acquisition parameters (sequence, TR, TE, flip angle) and scanner distribution across timepoints.
nm4_image_acquisition_protocol.supporting_text: “Three scanners at Oslo University Hospital were used… 1.5 Tesla Siemens MANETOM Sonata… MPRAGE… TR = 2.730 ms, TE = 3.93 ms, FA = 7°… 3 Tesla GE Signa HDxT… FSPGR… TR = 7.8 ms, TE = 3.18 ms, FA = 12°… 3 Tesla GE 750 Discovery… BRAVO… TR = 8.16 ms, TE = 3.18 ms, FA = 12°.”

nm5_data_preprocessing.reason: Preprocessing used FreeSurfer v5.3 with Destrieux atlas parcellation, and automatic quality control based on the Euler characteristic removed scans with Euler >5.
nm5_data_preprocessing.supporting_text: “T1-weighted structural MRI scans were preprocessed through Freesurfer (version 5.3), and CT measures were parcellated using the Destrieux atlas… An automatic quality check procedure based on the Freesurfer Euler characteristic was run on all data and samples with a value higher than 5 were removed.”

nm6_internal_data_validation_reference_c.reason: The normative models were trained on 95% of 40,435 participants and validated on an independent 5% (2,548) hold-out set stratified by site; adaptation used held-out cross-sectional controls for the Oslo scanners.
nm6_internal_data_validation_reference_c.supporting_text: “the reference normative models were first trained on (95%) healthy individuals and validated on an independent set of 2548 CTRL and patients (5%, stratified by sites). We then adapted the model to the 3 unseen Oslo scanners… using held-out cross-sectional data from CTRL from these 3 scanners.”

nm7_external_data_validation_reference_c.reason: Aside from the internal hold-out split and adaptation with local controls, no independent external healthy dataset was used to test the normative model; external validation is not reported.
nm7_external_data_validation_reference_c.supporting_text: No application of the model to an independent external healthy dataset beyond the internal 5% validation and local adaptation is described.

nm8_normative_modeling_approach.reason: They used hierarchical Bayesian regression normative models per ROI with age as covariate and sex/scanner as batch effects, employing transfer learning to adapt to new scanners.
nm8_normative_modeling_approach.supporting_text: “we used the Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) approach for normative modeling… We estimated a normative model for each region of interest… using HBR with age as a covariate, and sex and scanner id as batch effects… We then adapted the model to the 3 unseen Oslo scanners, by transferring the (hyper) parameters as informed priors.”

nm9_model_performance_reference_cohort.reason: They mention a 95%/5% train–validation split but do not report quantitative performance metrics (e.g., error, variance explained) for the reference cohort.
nm9_model_performance_reference_cohort.supporting_text: “trained on (95%) healthy individuals and validated on an independent set of 2548 CTRL and patients (5%, stratified by sites).”

nm10_characteristics_reference_cohort_ea.reason: Partitioning is described (95% training, 5% validation with 2,548 participants), but demographic characteristics for each partition are not provided.
nm10_characteristics_reference_cohort_ea.supporting_text: “reference normative models were first trained on (95%) healthy individuals and validated on an independent set of 2548 CTRL and patients (5%, stratified by sites).”

nm11_reproducibility.reason: Key software and model details are given (FreeSurfer v5.3, Destrieux atlas, hierarchical Bayesian regression with specified covariates and transfer learning), but code/model availability, software library versions beyond FreeSurfer, and data access are not provided.
nm11_reproducibility.supporting_text: “preprocessed through Freesurfer (version 5.3)… Destrieux atlas… we used the Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR)… using HBR with age as a covariate, and sex and scanner id as batch effects… adapted the model to the 3 unseen Oslo scanners.”

cr1_selection_criteria_clinical_cohort.reason: Clinical participants were first-episode schizophrenia spectrum patients recruited from Oslo hospitals with SCID-IV diagnoses, language/IQ/head trauma criteria, and exclusion of severe substance or mental illness history; healthy controls had psychiatric/substance exclusions. MRI QC excluded poor scans, and final sample sizes per wave are provided.
cr1_selection_criteria_clinical_cohort.supporting_text: “patients with a first-episode schizophrenia spectrum diagnosis… recruited… diagnosis… using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I Disorders… Healthy CTRL… Exclusion criteria for healthy CTRL included a history of drug or alcohol abuse or dependency, psychosis, bipolar disorder, or major depressive disorder” / “understood and spoke a Scandinavian language, had no history of severe head trauma, and had an IQ above 70… excluded… severe mental illness or… severe substance or alcohol abuse.” / “samples with a value higher than 5 were removed.” / “N 218…79…67…23”

cr2_handling_of_clinical_covariates.reason: Analyses of PANSS scores modeled time since inclusion, age at baseline, and sex; no clinical covariates beyond basic demographics (e.g., medication status, illness duration) were incorporated.
cr2_handling_of_clinical_covariates.supporting_text: “we used an LME model to assess the change in PANSS subscales over time, while controlling for age at baseline and sex.”

cr3_data_sources_clinical_cohort.reason: Clinical participants were drawn from the TOP study at the University of Oslo/Oslo University Hospital between October 2004 and October 2012, with recruitment sites listed.
cr3_data_sources_clinical_cohort.supporting_text: “All participants were recruited to a specific first-episode sub-study of the TOP study at the University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital from October 27, 2004, to October 17, 2012… recruited from… inpatient and outpatient services at Oslo University Hospital and 3 additional hospitals in the larger Oslo area.”

cr4_clinical_characteristics_clinical_co.reason: Sample sizes and demographics by timepoint are given in Table 1, and medication use proportions across visits are summarized.
cr4_clinical_characteristics_clinical_co.supporting_text: “N 218…79…197…67…77…23” / “Age, mean [SD]… Sex ratio (female)” / “patients primarily used second-generation antipsychotics (62% at baseline, 48% at 1 year, and 17% at 10 years) or did not use any antipsychotics (38%, 50%, and 83%).”

cr5_clinical_assessment_measures.reason: Diagnoses were established with SCID-IV, and clinical symptoms were measured with the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) at each timepoint.
cr5_clinical_assessment_measures.supporting_text: “Psychiatric diagnosis at baseline was established using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV Axis I Disorders (SCID-I)… Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores were acquired at each timepoint.”

cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.reason: They defined extreme deviations as |z|>2 and interpreted negative deviations as greater symptom severity in specific regions, reporting associations with PANSS domains and attenuation over time.
cr6_interpretation_of_deviation_scores.supporting_text: “We defined the threshold for extreme deviation values as | z | > 2.0.” / “Anterior cingulate gyrus was associated with PANSS total and PANSS general… insula… medial orbital sulcus… associated with PANSS negative. Negative associations indicate more negative deviation scores with higher symptom severity.” / “differences evident in the deviations at the first timepoint attenuate at later timepoints.”
